"text": "CRITICAL UX FAILURE & EXECUTIVE ACTION REQUIRED: Restoring Fundamental Watch Behavior via Adaptive Power\nDear Samsung Electronics Executive Leadership (Product Strategy
column6:
I would like to raise a critical user experience issue affecting the Galaxy Watch series.
This is not a feature request.
This is a fundamental usability issue affecting the core purpose of a watch.
Core Problem: The Removal of Raise to Wake
A watch
column7: regardless of how advanced its technology may be
column8: exists primarily for one essential purpose:\nIt must show the time immediately when the user looks at it.\nFor decades
column9: the natural interaction between a person and a watch has remained unchanged. The user raises their wrist
column11:
and instantly sees the time.
Galaxy Watch successfully modernized this behavior through Raise to Wake.
This feature is not merely a convenience. It is one of the foundational interactions of the entire Galaxy Watch experience.
The watch detects intentional wrist movement and immediately presents information without requiring any additional action.
This behavior is what makes a smartwatch feel like a watch.
Currently
column12: when Power Saving Mode is enabled
column13: Raise to Wake becomes unavailable.\nThis creates a contradiction.\nPower Saving Mode is designed for situations where battery life becomes most valuable. Ironically
column14: these are also the moments when users need the fastest and most efficient access to the time.\nInstead of simply raising their wrist
column15: users must touch the display or press a button.\nAt that moment
column16:
the device no longer behaves like a watch.
It behaves like a powered-down electronic device requiring manual activation.
Why This Creates UX Friction
Checking the time is one of the most frequent interactions performed on any watch.
Users may perform this action dozens or even hundreds of times per day.
Every additional tap
column18:
or interaction introduces friction into what should be an effortless experience.
The issue becomes particularly noticeable during:
• Walking  • Driving  • Exercising  • Carrying objects  • Outdoor activities  • Professional work environments
In these situations
column19:
Raise to Wake is not a luxury feature.
It is the expected behavior of a watch.
The Contradiction of Power Saving Mode
Power Saving Mode should reduce non-essential power consumption.
However
column20: Raise to Wake is not a non-essential function.\nIt is the mechanism through which the watch fulfills its primary purpose.\nReducing animations
column25:
and other power-intensive processes is understandable.
Removing immediate access to the time is not.
A watch that cannot conveniently show the time when the user raises their wrist undermines the fundamental reason the product is worn in the first place.
Recommended Solution: Adaptive Power Mode
Samsung could implement an Adaptive Power approach where:
• Raise to Wake remains available  • Display-on duration is shortened  • Animations are simplified  • Refresh rates are reduced  • Background activity is further optimized  • Non-critical functions remain restricted
This would preserve battery life while maintaining the fundamental identity of the product.
Strategic Business Impact
This change would:
• Improve daily usability  • Reduce user frustration  • Increase customer satisfaction  • Strengthen ecosystem loyalty  • Improve perceived software intelligence  • Reinforce Samsung's reputation for thoughtful UX design
Most importantly
column26:
it would preserve the defining interaction that makes Galaxy Watch feel like a watch.
Conclusion
Power Saving Mode should never remove the most essential interaction of a watch.
A user should always be able to raise their wrist and immediately see the time.
Raise to Wake is not a premium feature.
It is not an optional convenience.
It is one of the core foundations of the Galaxy Watch experience.
I respectfully ask Samsung's Product
column28: and Engineering teams to review this behavior and consider restoring Raise to Wake functionality within Power Saving Mode through an adaptive implementation.\nThank you for your time
column30: and continued commitment to improving the Galaxy Watch platform."

column2: "text": "@samsung Combining a wide f/1.4 aperture with a large sensor like the 1/1.12\" or 1/1.28\" is essentially the \"Holy Grail\" of mobile photography. When you pair a massive physical opening with a massive surface area for catching light
column3:
you move away from "phone quality" and start approaching the physics of dedicated mirrorless cameras.
​Here is what happens when those two specific technologies collide:
​1. Extreme Light Gathering (The "Night Owl" Effect)
​The most immediate benefit is low-light performance.
​Sensor Size: A 1/1.12" sensor has much larger individual pixels (or "super-pixels" when binning) than a standard sensor.
​Aperture: The f/1.4 opening allows a massive volume of photons to hit those pixels.
Together
column5: clean images in environments where the human eye struggles to see
column6: reducing the need for aggressive \"Night Mode\" long exposures that often cause motion blur.\n​2. Natural Optical Bokeh\n​Most phones use software (AI) to blur the background in Portrait Mode. However
column7:
a large sensor combined with an f/1.4 aperture creates natural depth of field.
​The transition between the sharp subject and the blurred background (the "fall-off") is much smoother and more professional.
​You won't see those "cut-out" errors around hair or glasses that software often misses.
​3. The "Thin Focus" Challenge
​While bigger is usually better
column8: this combination introduces a specific technical hurdle: a very shallow plane of focus.\n​With a sensor as big as 1/1.12\" and an aperture at f/1.4
column9: the \"slice\" of the image that is in focus is extremely thin.\n​If you take a close-up photo of a person
column11: but their nose and ears could be blurred. This is why many manufacturers (like Huawei or Xiaomi) now use Variable Aperture—allowing the camera to stop down to f/4.0 when you need the whole scene to be sharp.\n​Comparison of Light Intake\n​To give you an idea of the scale
